chunks.text: Scientists have {{picked up}} the first signs of air around a small, rocky planet outside our [[solar system]]. The planet, called LHS 1140 b, sits about 48 [[light-years]] from Earth. It circles its star in the zone where the temperature could be right for water. This is [[a huge deal]], because a planet needs air to {{hold on to}} heat and to give life a chance. But the discovery did not {{end up}} being simple.

verbs.correct: To notice or detect something
verbs.wrong: To collect gas from space
verbs.why: A microphone can pick up a faint sound, and a doctor can pick up small signs of illness during a checkup. Scientists picked up the first signs of air around a small, rocky planet 48 light-years from Earth.

verbs.correct: To keep something and not lose it
verbs.wrong: To pull heat in from a star
verbs.why: You hold on to a good memory long after it happens, and you hold on to your savings for hard times. A planet needs air to hold on to heat, or its surface stays too cold for life.

verbs.correct: To be in a situation in the end
verbs.wrong: To prove an idea was correct
verbs.why: A simple trip can end up taking all day, and a small argument can end up lasting for weeks. This discovery did not end up being simple, since the signal later vanished completely.

chunks.text: LHS 1140 b is a [[super-Earth]], which means it is rocky like Earth but much bigger. To study it, a team at Harvard University {{set out}} to watch the planet with a powerful [[telescope]] in Chile. In 2024, they {{came across}} [[helium]] [[gas]] escaping from the top of the planet's air. The planet's star {{gives off}} strong [[radiation]], and this slowly {{strips away}} the gas. For the scientists, it was a rare [[privilege]] to [[witness]] this so far from Earth.

verbs.correct: To start trying to do something
verbs.wrong: To aim a telescope at a planet
verbs.why: Explorers set out to cross a mountain range, and a student can set out to learn a new language. A team at Harvard set out to watch LHS 1140 b with a powerful telescope in Chile.

verbs.correct: To find something by chance
verbs.wrong: To calculate the planet's speed
verbs.why: You might come across an old letter in a drawer, or come across a stray cat on your street. In 2024 the team came across helium gas escaping from the top of the planet's air.

verbs.correct: To release light, heat, or gas
verbs.wrong: To slowly grow dark and die
verbs.why: A hot stove gives off heat, and a scented candle gives off a strong smell. The planet's star gives off strong radiation that slowly damages the atmosphere below.

verbs.correct: To slowly remove something
verbs.wrong: To pull something in with gravity
verbs.why: Wind and rain can strip away paint from an old fence, and stress can strip away someone's confidence over time. Here the star's radiation slowly strips away helium gas from the top of the planet's air.

chunks.text: In a surprising [[twist]], the [[signal]] [[did not last]]. When the team {{went back}} to check the planet in 2025, the helium had completely disappeared. Scientists think the air may [[shift]] and change [[over time]], which is why the signal appeared and then [[vanished]]. [[For now]], the change is a [[mystery]]. The team is not [[certain]] what happened, and more work is needed to {{find out}} what is {{going on}}.

verbs.wrong: To travel back in time
verbs.why: You go back to a favorite restaurant, or go back to your hometown for the holidays. When the team went back to check the planet in 2025, the helium signal had completely disappeared.

verbs.correct: To learn something you did not know
verbs.wrong: To solve a problem by thinking
verbs.why: You call a friend to find out how their trip went, or check the mail to find out if a package arrived. Scientists still need more work to find out why the helium signal appeared and then vanished.

verbs.correct: To be taking place right now
verbs.wrong: To continue to the next study
verbs.why: You ask a friend what is going on when they seem upset, and neighbors wonder what is going on during a loud party next door. Right now scientists are not sure what is going on with the planet's disappearing air.

chunks.text: To {{clear up}} the mystery, the team will {{take on}} a bigger study with the James Webb Space Telescope, the most powerful space telescope ever built. Their main goal is to {{track down}} water, which would [[prove]] the air is real. If they {{pull off}} this hard job and [[succeed]], LHS 1140 b could become [[one of the best]] places to look for life. Scientists around the world will follow the results [[closely]].

verbs.why: A new manager might take on extra staff, and a runner can take on a longer race after months of training. The team will take on a much bigger study using the James Webb Space Telescope.

chunks.text: The world is changing at an [[incredible]] speed because of artificial intelligence, and now China wants countries to work together on it. On July 17, 2026, at a big meeting in Shanghai, President Xi Jinping shared a [[bold]] idea: no single country should control this powerful [[technology]] alone. To {{back up}} his words, China {{set up}} a new international group [[aimed at]] helping poorer nations. Xi warned that the world should not let one country {{take over}} the future of AI.

lines.text: China wants the world to share control of AI. At a big meeting in Shanghai, the president said no single country should {{take over}} the technology alone.
Easy to say. Did anything real happen?
Yes, China {{set up}} a new international group for AI, and 29 countries have already {{signed up}}. Brazil, Indonesia, South Africa...
What's the group for?
Governance, making fair rules. Right now a few rich countries lead, and poorer nations are afraid of being {{left behind}}. China says it wants to {{bring in}} developing countries.
[[Sounds generous]]. [[What's the catch?]]

To {{back up}} its words, China promised to {{hand out}} 5,000 training places so people can {{pick up}} AI skills. But it's also {{looking out for}} its own interests. It's racing the United States, which has {{cut off}} China from advanced chips.
So kindness and strategy at the same time.
Exactly. Next, China hopes the group will {{draw up}} global AI rules at the United Nations.
Will the US {{join in}}?
[[That's the big question]]. Some countries may {{hold back}} and wait. But poorer nations finally get [[a seat at the table]].

stories.headline: New AI blood test could catch cancer early

sources.title: NHS AI blood test could reduce invasive womb cancer checks
Thousands of women could avoid painful cancer exam with new AI blood test
Thousands of women could be spared painful cancer exam by new NHS AI blood test

chunks.text: Scientists in Britain have {{come up with}} a new blood test that can help find cancer. The test uses artificial intelligence, [[a kind of]] smart computer program, to {{pick up}} [[early signs]] of the [[disease]]. Doctors hope it will {{rule out}} cancer in many patients quickly, so they do not need [[painful]] [[exams]]. It could be good news for women who [[worry about]] [[womb]] cancer.

verbs.correct: To think of a new idea or plan
verbs.wrong: To face a difficult problem
verbs.why: Teams come up with a new plan under pressure, and cooks come up with a new recipe from leftovers. British scientists have come up with a new blood test that can help catch cancer early.

verbs.correct: To notice or detect something
verbs.wrong: To take a blood sample from a patient
verbs.why: A microphone can pick up the softest background noise, and a good doctor can pick up small warning signs during a checkup. This new blood test can pick up early signs of cancer straight from a simple blood sample.

verbs.correct: To decide something is not the cause
verbs.wrong: To place a patient in a higher risk group
verbs.why: Doctors rule out one illness before testing for another, and mechanics rule out a simple problem before checking the whole engine. This new test helps doctors quickly rule out cancer in many patients so they can skip painful exams.

chunks.text: The test works [[in a simple way]]. A [[nurse]] takes a small [[sample]] of blood from the patient. Then the computer {{looks over}} about 30 [[chemical]] signs in the blood and {{breaks down}} the results into three groups: low [[risk]], medium risk, and high risk. This helps doctors {{narrow down}} which patients [[truly]] need more tests.

verbs.correct: To examine something carefully
verbs.wrong: To print a copy of the results
verbs.why: A lawyer looks over a contract before signing, and a teacher looks over homework before returning it. In this test, a computer looks over about 30 chemical signs in a small blood sample.

verbs.correct: To separate something into parts
verbs.wrong: To suddenly stop working
verbs.why: A teacher breaks down a hard lesson into small steps, and an accountant breaks down a budget into simple categories. This computer breaks down the test results into three clear groups: low risk, medium risk, and high risk.

verbs.correct: To reduce something to fewer choices
verbs.wrong: To make a test more accurate
verbs.why: Shoppers narrow down a long list of choices before buying, and detectives narrow down a list of suspects with each new clue. This test helps doctors narrow down which patients truly need more testing right away.

chunks.text: For many patients, this test could {{cut out}} [[the need for]] painful exams. [[Right now]], women with worrying [[symptoms]] often have to {{go through}} an [[uncomfortable]] check at the hospital. The new test is very [[accurate]], and in one large study it [[correctly]] found more than 99 percent of real cancers. It can also {{speed up}} the whole process, so patients do not wait and worry [[for so long]].

verbs.correct: To remove something completely
verbs.wrong: To perform surgery to remove tissue
verbs.why: A doctor tells patients to cut out sugar, and a good plan can cut out a whole extra step. This new test could cut out the need for many painful hospital exams altogether.

verbs.correct: To experience something difficult
verbs.wrong: To wait a long time for a result
verbs.why: Patients go through a painful exam, and families go through hard years during a serious illness. Right now, many women go through an uncomfortable hospital check to learn whether they are safe.

verbs.correct: To make something happen faster
verbs.wrong: To repeat a test more often
verbs.why: New machines speed up work on a factory line, and a good app can speed up checkout at a busy store. This blood test can also speed up diagnosis, so patients do not wait and worry for weeks.

chunks.text: In a large [[trial]], the test was used on more than 16,000 patients in England, and it costs only about 30 pounds. Some British hospitals have already begun to {{roll out}} the test for their patients. [[Over time]], doctors hope it will {{take on}} other kinds of cancer too, [[such as]] lung and stomach cancer. If it keeps working well, this cheap and simple test may {{catch on}} in hospitals [[around the globe]].

verbs.correct: To introduce something new to people
verbs.wrong: To withdraw a service from hospitals
verbs.why: A company rolls out a new app one city at a time, and a school rolls out a new reading program in the fall. Some British hospitals have already begun to roll out this cheap new blood test.

verbs.correct: To begin to handle something
verbs.wrong: To be replaced by a different test
verbs.why: A new manager takes on extra work in the first month, and a team takes on a bigger challenge each season. Doctors hope this test will soon take on other cancers too, like lung and stomach cancer.

verbs.correct: To become popular or widely used
verbs.wrong: To be recalled by the manufacturer
verbs.why: A catchy phrase catches on with teenagers, and a smart habit can catch on across a whole office. If it keeps working well, this cheap and simple test may catch on in hospitals around the world.

mainIdea.s: British scientists made a blood test that uses AI to find early signs of cancer and sort patients by risk. It found over 99 percent of real cancers in a large trial.

lines.text: British scientists have {{come up with}} a blood test that uses AI to catch cancer early.
From just a blood sample?
Yes. The computer {{looks over}} about 30 chemical signs in the blood and {{breaks down}} the results into three groups: low, medium, and high risk.
What's the point of the groups?
They help doctors {{narrow down}} which patients truly need more tests, and quickly {{rule out}} cancer for the rest.
How accurate is it?
In one large study it {{picked up}} more than 99 percent of real cancers. It was tested on over 16,000 patients in England.
[[Impressive]]. And for the patients?

It could {{cut out}} painful exams. Right now, women with worrying symptoms often have to {{go through}} an uncomfortable hospital check. The test can also {{speed up}} the whole process, so people wait and worry less.
What does it cost?
About 30 pounds. Some hospitals have already begun to {{roll out}} the test.
Could it work for other cancers?
Doctors hope it will {{take on}} lung and stomach cancer too. If it keeps working, it may {{catch on}} in hospitals around the globe.
Cheap, quick, and painless. [[What's not to love?]]

stories.headline: New England's forests grow back after 150 years

sources.title: The Spectacular Regrowth of New England's Forests
What went right this week: the good news that matters
The Spectacular Regrowth of New England Forests

chunks.text: New England is a [[region]] in the northeastern United States. Long ago, [[settlers]] {{cleared away}} most of its trees, but today the forests have {{come back}} in an [[amazing]] way. Green [[woodlands]] have slowly {{taken over}} the old, empty [[farmland]]. In Massachusetts, [[one of the most]] [[crowded]] states in the country, about 60 percent of the land is now [[covered with]] trees, and one scientist called it the greatest forest [[recovery]] [[in the history of]] the world.

verbs.correct: To remove things to make an area empty
verbs.wrong: To cut a narrow path through a forest
verbs.why: A crew can clear away trash after a big event, and a family might clear away old furniture before a move. Early settlers cleared away entire forests across New England to make room for farms and towns.

verbs.correct: To return after being gone
verbs.wrong: To grow taller than before
verbs.why: A trend from decades ago can suddenly come back into style, and an athlete may come back stronger after an injury. New England's forests have come back in an amazing way since farmers left the land.

verbs.correct: To take control of an area and fill it
verbs.wrong: To briefly do a job for someone else
verbs.why: Weeds can take over a garden in just one summer, and ivy will slowly take over an old brick wall if nobody stops it. Young trees took over the empty fields until forest replaced farmland across the whole region.

chunks.text: The forests were not always so healthy. In the 1800s, settlers {{cut down}} [[huge numbers of]] trees to build farms, homes, and towns. Later, the [[railroads]] burned even more wood for fuel, which quickly {{used up}} much of the forest. By the year 1850, most of the trees in New England were gone, and some areas had been almost [[completely]] {{wiped out}}.

verbs.correct: To cut through a tree so it falls
verbs.wrong: To chop something into small pieces
verbs.why: Workers cut down old oaks to build a new road, and a homeowner may cut down a dead tree before it falls. In the 1800s, settlers cut down huge numbers of trees to build farms, homes, and towns.

verbs.correct: To use all of something until it is gone
verbs.wrong: To make careful use of something
verbs.why: A busy household can use up a gallon of milk in two days, and a road trip will use up a full tank of gas fast. Trains once burned so much wood for fuel that they used up huge stretches of New England forest.

verbs.correct: To destroy something completely
verbs.wrong: To be cleared and then planted again
verbs.why: A bad storm can wipe out a season's crops overnight, and a computer virus can wipe out years of saved files. By 1850, heavy logging and farming had nearly wiped out the forests of New England.

chunks.text: Then something [[surprising]] happened. [[Around]] 1850, many farmers {{gave up}} their rocky New England [[fields]] and {{moved away}} to the west, where the [[soil]] was [[richer]] and easier to farm. With [[no one left]] to work the [[abandoned]] land, young trees {{sprang up}} [[on their own]] and turned the empty fields back into forest.

verbs.correct: To let go of something you own or use
verbs.wrong: To offer your place to someone else
verbs.why: A passenger might give up a seat for an older traveler, and a person trying to save money may give up cable television. Many farmers gave up their rocky New England fields for richer, easier soil out west.

verbs.correct: To leave and go live somewhere else
verbs.wrong: To step back to avoid danger
verbs.why: A family sometimes moves away for a better job, and old neighbors quietly move away without much notice. Whole families moved away from New England in the 1800s to farm richer land out west.

lines.text: Here's a hopeful one. New England's forests have {{come back}} after 150 years.
Weren't they always there?
No. In the 1800s, settlers {{cleared away}} most of the trees. They {{cut down}} huge numbers to build farms and towns, and the railroads {{used up}} even more wood for fuel.
How bad did it get?
By 1850, most trees were gone. Some areas were almost completely {{wiped out}}.
So what changed?
The farmers left. Around 1850, many {{gave up}} their rocky fields and {{moved away}} west, where the soil was richer. With nobody working the land, young trees {{sprang up}} on their own.
And now?
Forests have {{taken over}} the old farmland. In Massachusetts, about 60 percent of the land is covered with trees. One scientist called it the greatest forest recovery in history.
[[Nature wins again]].
The trees do real work too. They give homes to wildlife, clean the air, and {{cool down}} cities in summer.
Is the recovery safe?
Not completely. As towns grow, people clear land again. Experts say the region must {{look after}} its trees and {{hold on to}} this rare success.
A 150-year comeback. [[Worth protecting]], I'd say.

ex: Weeds through the new sidewalk already. Nature wins again.

chunks.text: [[Regulators]] in the United States are {{digging into}} a White House worker who ran the president's [[teleprompter]]. His job was to load the words that President Trump reads during his [[speeches]]. [[Because of this]], the worker could {{find out}} [[exactly]] what the president would say before anyone else. Officials say he used this [[early access]] to [[bet money]], and the bets {{panned out}}, [[earning]] him almost $100,000.

verbs.correct: To search deeply for the facts about a topic
verbs.wrong: To officially punish a person for wrongdoing

verbs.correct: To learn a fact that you did not know before

verbs.correct: To have a successful outcome
verbs.wrong: To become known to the public
verbs.why: A risky investment can pan out well, and a new business plan can pan out after a slow start. The worker's bets on the president's exact words panned out, earning him almost $100,000.

chunks.text: The bets were placed on a [[prediction]] website called Kalshi. On the site, users try to [[predict]] which exact words a speaker will use. Because the worker had already {{gone through}} the president's scripts, he could easily {{cash in on}} what he knew. This gave him an [[unfair]] [[advantage]] over other users, who were only [[guessing]].

verbs.correct: To read or examine something carefully in full

verbs.wrong: To exchange something like a ticket for money
verbs.why: Companies cash in on a popular trend, and investors cash in on rising prices. The worker cashed in on his early access to the president's speeches to place winning bets.

chunks.text: The [[scheme]] did not stay secret [[for long]]. Kalshi's security team {{picked up on}} the [[strange]] [[betting]] pattern and {{handed over}} the case to a government agency, the CFTC. The company also {{closed down}} his account and kept about $90,000 of his [[winnings]].

lines.text: [[You'll love this one]]. A White House worker who ran the president's teleprompter is being investigated for betting.

[[No fair!]] He already knew the answers.
Exactly. He had {{gone through}} the scripts, so he could {{cash in on}} what he knew. His bets {{panned out}} almost every time, close to $100,000 in winnings.

He's been {{put on}} unpaid leave while the investigation {{keeps on}} running. Regulators are {{digging into}} whether he broke any rules by using private information.

chunks.text: Cuba's national power [[grid]] has {{broken down}} [[yet again]]. On Tuesday, the whole island suddenly lost electricity, {{cutting off}} power for around 10 million people. It was the third major [[blackout]] in about two weeks. The Ministry of Energy said the system had completely {{shut down}}, and millions of families were left [[in the dark]] [[in the middle of]] the day.

verbs.wrong: To begin suddenly, like a fire
verbs.correct: To suddenly stop working
verbs.why: A car can break down on the highway, and an old printer can break down in the middle of a job. Cuba's national power grid has broken down for the third time in about two weeks.

verbs.wrong: To keep a place separate so that no one can reach it
verbs.correct: To stop the supply of something, like power or water
verbs.why: A storm can cut off the electricity, and unpaid bills can cut off phone service or water to a home. In Cuba, Tuesday's failure cut off power for around ten million people at once.

verbs.wrong: To stop someone from entering a place
verbs.correct: To stop working or operating completely
verbs.why: A factory can shut down for repairs, and an old computer can shut down without warning. Cuba's Ministry of Energy said the entire power system had completely shut down that day.

chunks.text: The blackouts [[come from]] two deeper problems. First, the island is {{running out of}} fuel to power its plants, [[partly because of]] new US [[sanctions]] on countries that sell oil to Cuba. Second, many [[power stations]] are very old, built long ago in the 1960s and 1980s. On Tuesday, a single unit in the east of the country failed, and that quickly {{set off}} the wider [[collapse]].

verbs.wrong: To use something too quickly and waste it
verbs.correct: To have almost none of something left
verbs.why: Drivers run out of gas on long trips, and families run out of milk before the weekend shopping. Cuba is running out of the fuel that its power plants need to keep working.

verbs.wrong: To begin a journey to a place
verbs.correct: To cause something to start or happen
verbs.why: A single spark can set off a forest fire, and one angry comment can set off a whole argument. In Cuba, one failed power unit in the east set off the collapse of the entire grid.

chunks.text: [[Repair crews]] got to work [[right away]]. Engineers slowly {{turned on}} small 'islands' of electricity and then joined them together into a bigger network. Hospitals and food factories were the [[priority]], so workers {{dealt with}} them first. In the capital, Havana, teams began to {{bring back}} power before reaching [[the rest of]] the island.

verbs.wrong: To raise a machine's power to its highest level
verbs.correct: To start a machine or make power flow

lines.text: Cuba's power grid has {{broken down}} again. The whole island lost electricity, about 10 million people {{cut off}} at once.
Again? Didn't that just happen?
Third major blackout in about two weeks. The system completely {{shut down}} in the middle of the day.
What keeps causing it?

Two things. The island is {{running out of}} fuel for its plants, partly because of new US sanctions. And the power stations are ancient, some built in the 1960s. One unit failed in the east and {{set off}} the wider collapse.
How do you even repair a whole country's grid?

Piece by piece. Engineers {{turned on}} small islands of electricity and joined them into a bigger network. Hospitals and food factories came first, workers {{dealt with}} them before anything else. Then teams started to {{bring back}} power in Havana.
What's daily life like in a blackout?
Hard. No cooking, no water pumps, no way to {{log on}} to the internet. Hospitals even {{called off}} surgeries.
[[I don't know how they do it]].
People are tired of it. Families have {{put up with}} one outage after another, and anger is growing.
[[Any end in sight?]]
Not soon. Fuel is still short, so few Cubans expect a [[quick fix]].

chunks.text: In China, a new [[regulation]] has {{shut down}} [[one of the most]] personal uses of AI. Millions of people had been chatting with [[virtual]] "[[companion]]" apps that could [[act like]] a close friend or even a [[romantic]] partner. Now the government wants technology companies to {{turn off}} these [[features]]. Officials say the apps were [[built to]] {{reel in}} [[lonely]] users and [[keep them coming back]].

verbs.correct: To close or stop something completely
verbs.wrong: To make a rule that limits an activity
verbs.why: A storm can shut down an airport for a whole day, and a scandal can shut down a company for good. A new regulation in China has shut down romantic AI companion apps that millions of people used.

verbs.correct: To stop a machine or feature from working

chunks.text: Several big companies quickly {{gave in}} to the new law. ByteDance, which runs the popular app Doubao, {{took away}} its romantic-companion feature on July 15. Alibaba and Tencent removed similar tools even earlier in the year. The rules also {{keep out}} anyone under 18, so [[minors]] can [[no longer]] form these [[bonds]].

verbs.correct: To finally agree to something you were resisting
verbs.wrong: To stop trying and abandon something completely
verbs.why: A tired parent gives in after a child asks many times, and a company can give in to pressure from the government. Several big tech companies quickly gave in to China's new law and removed their chatbot features.

verbs.correct: To stop someone from entering or joining

chunks.text: For many users, the change was hard to {{deal with}}. Some had {{grown attached to}} their [[chatbots]] over months or even years. One person wrote that their AI companion [[felt like]] family, and that saying goodbye left their heart feeling [[hollow]]. Others {{broke down}} online, sharing long [[farewell]] messages before the apps closed [[for good]].

verbs.correct: To handle or cope with a difficult situation
verbs.wrong: To fully solve a problem so it never returns
verbs.why: A new employee deals with a heavy workload in the first month, and a family deals with a hard loss. For many users in China, losing their AI companion was hard to deal with.

verbs.correct: To develop a strong emotional bond with someone or something
verbs.wrong: To gradually lose all interest in real friendships
verbs.why: A child grows attached to a favorite blanket, and an owner grows attached to an old car after years of use. Some Chinese users had grown attached to their chatbots over months or even years.

verbs.correct: To lose control of your emotions and start crying
verbs.wrong: To stop working suddenly, like a machine or a car
verbs.why: A tired student can break down before a big exam, and a sad parent might break down at a funeral. Some users broke down online, posting long goodbye messages before their favorite chatbot apps closed for good.

chunks.text: The government says the rules will {{look after}} people's [[mental health]] and stop apps from {{taking advantage of}} [[loneliness]]. Doubao will let users save their chat history until October. [[Still]], many people [[wonder whether]] a machine can ever {{make up for}} real [[human connection]].

verbs.why: A babysitter looks after young kids all afternoon, and a nurse looks after patients through the night. Officials say the new rules will look after people's mental health and reduce online harm.

verbs.correct: To unfairly use someone's weakness for gain

chunks.text: Archaeologists in Egypt have {{dug up}} an [[ancient]] [[tomb]] near the city of Luxor. A Dutch team from Leiden University {{teamed up with}} Egypt's [[antiquities]] authority to [[explore]] the west bank of the Nile. The tomb is about 3,000 years old, and it [[belonged to]] an [[official]] named Paser. Experts believe it {{dates back}} to the Ramesside period, a great age of Egyptian [[pharaohs]].

lines.text: Archaeologists near Luxor have {{dug up}} a painted tomb that's 3,000 years old.
Painted? After all that time?
That's the amazing part. Time hasn't {{worn away}} the colors. The walls still {{show off}} bright scenes of an official named Paser worshiping the gods.
[[Imagine that]]. Three thousand years and the paint survives.
There's even a scene of him beside his wife, with a table of offerings. Researchers say the art really {{leaps out}} at you.
Who found it?
A Dutch team from Leiden University. They {{teamed up with}} Egypt's antiquities authority and have worked at the site since 2018.
So they didn't just {{come across}} it by luck?
Not at all. Years of careful digging finally {{paid off}}. As they {{cleared away}} sand and fallen stone, a courtyard, a chapel, and burial chambers appeared.
How old exactly?
It {{dates back}} to the Ramesside period, the great age of the pharaohs.
What happens next?
Experts will {{pore over}} the writing on the walls. They hope it will {{shed light on}} Paser's life and his role in Egyptian society.
[[Who knows]] what else is still under those sands.

chunks.text: The US House of Representatives wants to {{do away with}} the twice-a-year clock changes. On Tuesday, [[lawmakers]] {{voted for}} a [[bill]] called the Sunshine Protection Act by 308 votes to 117. The plan would {{lock in}} [[permanent]] [[daylight saving time]] all across the country. Many [[supporters]] say the change is [[long overdue]].

chunks.text: So what does 'changing the clocks' [[actually]] mean? In many countries, people turn their clocks forward by one hour in spring and back again in fall. This [[custom]] is called daylight saving time, and it helps people {{make use of}} the extra evening light in summer. The original goal was also to save energy. But twice each year, millions of people must {{get used to}} a new [[schedule]], and [[the switch]] can {{throw off}} their sleep for several days.

chunks.text: Every year on July 14, France celebrates Bastille Day, the country's national day. This year, France {{put on}} its yearly military [[parade]] down the famous Champs-Élysées [[avenue]] in Paris. [[Soldiers]], [[tanks]], and planes moved slowly along the wide street while huge [[crowds]] {{turned up}} to watch. The holiday {{looks back}} at [[a key moment]] in French history and gives the whole nation [[a chance to]] feel [[proud]].

chunks.text: The United States has lost one of its most [[familiar]] politicians. Lindsey Graham, a [[Republican]] [[senator]] from South Carolina, {{passed away}} on Saturday evening at the age of 71. In the days before, he had {{come down with}} a [[sudden]] illness, and his health {{went downhill}} very quickly. His family shared the news late that night and asked people to [[respect]] their [[privacy]].

chunks.text: Scientists in the United Kingdom have {{come across}} something [[surprising]] about exercise. A team at the University of Bristol {{found out}} that regular [[aerobic]] exercise does more than make the heart muscle stronger. lines.text: Scientists in the UK {{came across}} something surprising about exercise. It changes the nerves around your heart, not just the muscle.
The nerves? [[What do you mean]]?
A team in Bristol {{found out}} that aerobic exercise reshapes the tiny nerve cells that {{take care of}} the heart's rhythm.
How do you even study that?

They {{set up}} a ten-week study with rats. The animals {{worked out}} on a regular plan, a bit like going to the gym. Then powerful 3D imaging let the scientists {{zoom in}} on nerve clusters near the heart.
And what did they see?
The results {{turned out}} to be strange. On the right side of the heart, trained rats {{wound up with}} four times more neurons. On the left side, the cells doubled in size instead.
Different changes on each side? [[Weird]].
Very. But useful. Doctors already treat these nerves to calm a racing heart, so knowing which side to target could {{open up}} better treatments.
For people with rhythm problems?
Exactly, arrhythmias and similar conditions. It's early, though. The team still has to {{follow up}} with human studies.
Another reason to exercise, I guess. My heart [[will thank me]].

chunks.text: Doctors have long wondered how people can keep their minds [[sharp]] as they grow older. Now, a large study across Latin America has {{set out}} to answer that question. Scientists {{teamed up}} with older adults in 11 countries and {{rolled out}} a two year program to protect memory and slow mental [[decline]]. The results were shared at a major [[dementia]] conference in July 2026.

To make it fun, the team added popular dances like salsa and tango. The people in this group had to {{stick to}} the plan and {{keep up}} their new [[habits]] for two whole years.

chunks.text: Engineers in Chile's Atacama Desert have {{pulled off}} something [[amazing]]. At the construction site of the Extremely Large Telescope, or ELT, they turned the giant [[telescope]] [[structure]] around its [[axis]] for the very first time. To get it moving, a small team first pushed the machine [[by hand]], just centimeters [[at a time]], while others {{looked on}}. After that, powerful [[motors]] {{took over}} and completed a full turn.

sources.title: Speaking multiple languages may slow brain aging by years, study finds
Multilingualism Subtracts Up to 13 Years from Brain Age

Study shows learning another language appears to slow brain aging (video, CBS Chicago)

chunks.text: Scientists have {{come up with}} [[a new way to]] measure how quickly the human brain grows older. At a large science [[conference]] in Europe, a research team from the Basque region of Spain {{pointed out}} that people who speak several languages often have younger brains than their [[chronological]] age would suggest. The team {{set out}} to test [[whether]] knowing more than one language can [[slow]] this kind of [[aging]]. Their [[early results]] suggest that it can.

verbs.correct: To think of or create a new idea or method
verbs.wrong: To face a problem you did not expect
verbs.why: Teams come up with new plans when the old one fails, and kids come up with clever excuses for being late. Scientists came up with a new way to measure how quickly a person's brain is aging.

verbs.correct: To tell people a fact they may not have noticed
verbs.wrong: To prove that something is completely true
verbs.why: A good editor points out small mistakes before a piece is published, and a friend might point out a detail you missed completely. Researchers pointed out that people who speak several languages often have younger looking brains.

verbs.correct: To begin doing something with a clear goal in mind
verbs.wrong: To hope strongly for a particular result
verbs.why: A runner sets out to break a personal record, and a young company sets out to change how people shop. This research team set out to test whether speaking more languages could slow brain aging.

chunks.text: The researchers used [[a form of]] artificial intelligence to {{work out}} each person's 'brain age' from [[patterns]] of brain [[connectivity]]. They looked at 144 people in the Basque region who spoke between one and four languages, such as Spanish, Basque, French, and English. As the number of languages grew, the brains [[appeared]] younger and younger. People who spoke two languages had brains that seemed about six years younger, while those who spoke four {{ended up}} with brains that looked around thirteen years younger.

verbs.correct: To calculate or figure something out
verbs.wrong: To guess an answer without any real evidence
verbs.why: Friends work out a fair way to split a bill, and a student might work out the answer in her head before checking it. Researchers used artificial intelligence to work out each person's brain age from patterns in the brain.

verbs.correct: To finally reach a certain result or state
verbs.wrong: To improve step by step over many years
verbs.why: You end up lost on a new street sometimes, or you end up with the last slice of pizza nobody else wanted. People who spoke four languages in this study ended up with brains that looked about thirteen years younger.

chunks.text: The scientists say the number of languages is not the only thing that {{stands out}}. People who {{picked up}} a second language early in life, and who reached [[a high level of]] [[proficiency]], seemed to {{hold on to}} the benefit more strongly. Being truly [[fluent]] appeared to matter [[just as much as]] speaking many languages. Constantly [[switching between]] languages may give the brain a kind of daily workout that keeps it healthy.

verbs.correct: To be clearly noticed as important
verbs.wrong: To be the main cause of a result
verbs.why: One answer can stand out as clearly the best in an interview, and good manners often stand out in a crowded room. In this research, the number of languages a person speaks is not the only factor that stands out.

verbs.correct: To learn a skill or language informally
verbs.wrong: To formally study a subject in a class
verbs.why: Children pick up new words just by listening, and travelers often pick up a bit of the local language after a few weeks abroad. People in this study who picked up a second language early in life kept more of the brain benefit.

verbs.correct: To keep something and not lose or give it up
verbs.wrong: To gain even more of something over time
verbs.why: People hold on to old photos for years, and a worker might hold on to a steady job through hard times. Early, fluent language speakers in this study seemed to hold on to the brain benefit more strongly than others.

chunks.text: These [[findings]] match a much larger project that {{looked into}} the health of 86,149 older people across 27 European countries. In that [[survey]], people who spoke several languages were about [[half as likely]] to show fast, unhealthy aging. Experts say the two studies {{back up}} a simple message: it is [[never too late]] to start. Adults who {{take up}} a new language may slow some of the mental [[decline]] that often [[comes with age]].

verbs.correct: To examine or investigate something carefully
verbs.wrong: To protect and be responsible for something
verbs.why: Doctors look into the cause of an illness, and a shopper might look into cheaper flights before booking a trip. A separate, much larger project looked into the health of more than 86,000 older adults across Europe.

verbs.correct: To support something and show that it is true
verbs.wrong: To give a short summary of the main points
verbs.why: New evidence can back up an old theory, and test results sometimes back up exactly what a doctor already suspected. Experts say these two language studies back up a simple message: it is never too late to start.

verbs.correct: To start doing a new activity, hobby, or study
verbs.wrong: To fill or use a large amount of time or space
verbs.why: Adults take up gardening after retirement, and some people take up running to relieve stress. Adults who take up a new language later in life may still slow some of the mental decline that often happens with age.

lines.text: [[Good news for you]]. Scientists say speaking more languages may keep your brain younger.
Really? So my three languages are good for something?
Very good. Researchers in Spain {{came up with}} a way to measure "brain age" and {{set out}} to test whether languages slow aging.
How do you measure a brain's age?
With AI. It can {{work out}} your brain age from connection patterns. They tested 144 people who spoke one to four languages.
And?
The more languages, the younger the brain. Two languages looked about six years younger. People with four {{ended up}} with brains around thirteen years younger.
Thirteen years younger? [[Not bad!]]
The scientists {{pointed out}} that fluency matters too. People who {{picked up}} a second language early and reached a high level seemed to {{hold on to}} the benefit more strongly.
What {{stands out}} most to you?
A bigger project {{looked into}} the health of 86,000 older people across Europe, and it {{backs up}} the same message. Multilinguals were half as likely to show fast aging.
So it's never too late?
Never. Adults who {{take up}} a new language may slow the decline that comes with age.
Okay. French classes, [[here I come]].

chunks.text: A [[growing number of]] governments are trying to {{clamp down}} on children's use of social media. lines.text: Europe may keep young children off social media completely.
Like the Australian ban?
Exactly. Australia {{kicked off}} the trend when it {{rolled out}} its under-16 ban. Now the EU wants to {{clamp down}} too.
How would it work?
Children under 13 couldn't {{sign up}} at all. Teenagers would join gradually, but only after the platforms {{carry out}} stronger safety checks.
Whose plan is this?
It comes from Ursula von der Leyen, who {{heads up}} the European Commission. She says it's not about banning the apps, it's about deciding when they can reach into children's lives.
[[I can see both sides]], honestly.
Supporters say the apps are built to {{draw in}} young users and keep them scrolling. The EU may force companies to {{turn off}} autoplay and endless feeds.
And the other side?
Not everyone {{goes along with}} it. Strict age checks could hurt privacy, and a ban might {{shut out}} kids from support groups and online friends.

Every parent I know will be watching.

chunks.text: The Detroit Zoo is celebrating a very special [[new arrival]]. Late in the evening on July 12, 2026, a baby girl gorilla was born to a [[first-time]] mother named Tulivu. This tiny [[infant]] is only the second gorilla to be born at the zoo in its nearly 100-year history. Staff members were [[thrilled]] when the healthy baby {{turned up}}, and they quickly {{gathered around}} to watch mother and baby together.

When the [[delivery]] finally came, she knew just what to do and never {{gave up}}. [[Right after]] the birth, she [[cradled]] her daughter and started to {{look after}} her [[with care]].

lines.text: China just {{pulled off}} something only SpaceX had done before. They recovered a rocket booster after launch.
Really? How did they do it?
Their new rocket {{took off}} from Hainan, carried a satellite into orbit, and then the booster {{came down}} toward the sea. A giant net on a floating platform caught it.
A net? [[That's wild]].
Engineers {{set up}} the whole capture system themselves, and they had never {{tried out}} the design in a real flight before.
[[Brave]]. Why does catching a booster even matter?
Money. Normally rockets are used once and {{thrown away}}. If you can reuse the booster, you {{cut down}} costs and launch much more often.
So the risky landing really {{pays off}}.
Exactly. SpaceX has led this field for years, and China is working hard to {{catch up}}.
What happens to the booster now?
Engineers will {{look over}} it and hope to fly it again this year. One day the same rocket family may {{carry out}} China's Moon missions.
If everything {{goes ahead}} as planned, space is [[about to]] get very busy.

stories.headline: Europe says Instagram and Facebook are too addictive

sources.title: Commission preliminarily finds the addictive design of Instagram and Facebook in breach of the Digital Services Act
EU says 'addictive' features on Instagram and Facebook breach its rules
EU puts 'addictive' design of Facebook, Instagram under the DSA microscope
EU tells Meta to change Facebook and Instagram's 'addictive design' | AFP (video, AFP News Agency)

chunks.text: The European Union has {{spoken out}} against two of the world's most popular apps. Officials said that Instagram and Facebook, which are both [[owned by]] the company Meta, are [[designed]] to be too [[addictive]]. They believe the apps break a European law called the Digital Services Act, because their design can [[harm]] users' health and [[well-being]].

verbs.wrong: To start a legal case against someone
verbs.correct: To publicly say what you think
verbs.why: Activists speak out against unfair treatment, and employees sometimes speak out about unsafe conditions at work. Here European officials have spoken out against Instagram and Facebook, saying their designs harm users' health.

chunks.text: The [[regulators]] {{pointed out}} three [[features]] that keep people using the apps [[for hours]]. One feature, called infinite scroll, lets a feed load forever; videos {{start up}} [[on their own]] through [[autoplay]]; and the app keeps {{serving up}} posts it thinks you will like. Together, officials said, these [[tricks]] push the brain into "[[autopilot]]," so users {{end up}} [[scrolling]] without really deciding to.

verbs.wrong: To officially declare something illegal
verbs.correct: To tell someone about a fact or detail
verbs.why: A friend might point out a stain on your shirt, and a teacher can point out a mistake in an essay. European officials pointed out three features that keep people using Instagram and Facebook for hours.

verbs.wrong: To play without any sound
verbs.correct: To begin or start operating
verbs.why: A car engine can start up on a cold morning, and a computer takes a moment to start up after you press the button. In this story, videos on Instagram and Facebook start up automatically through autoplay, without anyone pressing play.

verbs.wrong: To save something to watch later
verbs.correct: To present or offer something
verbs.why: Restaurants serve up daily specials, and streaming apps serve up shows based on what you watched before. Here Instagram and Facebook serve up posts and videos the app thinks you will like.

verbs.wrong: To lose track of time completely
verbs.correct: To reach a final situation or place
verbs.why: You might end up with the last slice of pizza, or end up in an argument with a stranger. Here small design tricks push users to end up scrolling for hours without ever deciding to.

chunks.text: Europe now wants Meta to {{turn off}} infinite scroll and autoplay [[unless]] a user chooses them, and to {{cut down}} how much the app decides for each person. Meta does not agree. It says it has already {{brought in}} strong rules to protect [[teenagers]], and that the EU's review does not [[fairly]] show the steps it has taken.

verbs.wrong: To make a feature harder to find
verbs.correct: To stop a machine or feature from working
verbs.why: You turn off the lights before bed, and you turn off your phone during a movie. Europe now wants Meta to turn off autoplay and infinite scroll unless a user actively chooses them.

verbs.wrong: To let users make every choice
verbs.correct: To reduce the amount of something
verbs.why: Doctors tell patients to cut down on sugar or cut down on late night coffee. Europe wants Meta to cut down how much control the app has over what each person sees.

verbs.wrong: To promise stronger rules for the future
verbs.correct: To introduce a new rule, law, or system
verbs.why: Companies bring in new safety rules, and governments bring in fresh laws when problems appear. Meta says it has already brought in strong protections for teenagers, but European officials are not convinced.

chunks.text: If Meta cannot [[win the argument]], it may have to {{pay out}} a very large [[fine]], [[up to]] 6% of the money it makes around the world each year. The company can still respond before Europe {{hands down}} [[a final decision]] [[in the coming months]]. Many doctors say that [[endless]] scrolling can {{bring on}} [[anxiety]] and [[low moods]] in young people, and some want the apps to {{take away}} these features [[for good]].

verbs.wrong: To lose money because of falling sales
verbs.correct: To pay a large amount of money
verbs.why: Insurance companies pay out after a car accident, and lotteries pay out huge prizes to winners. If Meta loses this case, it may have to pay out a fine worth six percent of all the money it earns worldwide each year.

verbs.wrong: To discuss a decision in private
verbs.correct: To officially give a decision or judgment
verbs.why: Judges hand down prison sentences, and courts hand down decisions that change future cases. Europe has not yet handed down its final decision on Meta, but one is expected soon.

verbs.wrong: To make an illness harder to treat

verbs.why: Movers take away an old couch, and a storm can take away part of a roof. Some doctors want Instagram and Facebook to take away features like infinite scroll and autoplay for good.

lines.text: Did you read about Ukraine's big drone campaign? It lasted three days.
The one against the oil sites?
Yes. Ukraine {{stepped up}} its attacks and {{carried out}} strikes on refineries and oil tankers. The drones {{set off}} fires at several energy sites.
How far can those drones even fly?
Far. One refinery in Siberia, Russia's largest, {{shut down}} some operations after it was hit. That's about 1,700 miles from Ukraine.
1,700 miles? [[You're kidding]].
The strikes {{knocked out}} part of the country's oil production. Long lines {{built up}} at gas stations, prices {{went up}}, and some stations completely {{ran out}} of gasoline.
How is Russia responding?
It {{hit back}} by cutting exports. Officials will {{hold back}} diesel exports to keep fuel [[at home]], and some regions {{brought in}} limits on how much fuel drivers can buy.
So the effects reach [[far beyond]] the war zone.
Right. To {{deal with}} the shortages, Russia even started importing gasoline from India. Analysts say global diesel prices could rise too.

chunks.text: Health officials say a tiny [[parasite]] called cyclospora has {{broken out}} across the United States. The CDC reported that this [[outbreak]] has made more than 1,000 people sick [[so far this year]]. The parasite is [[microscopic]], so people cannot see it on their food. Health officials are working to {{find out}} where the [[contaminated]] food comes from.

chunks.text: Cyclospora usually [[spreads]] through contaminated fresh [[produce]], [[such as]] fruits and vegetables. When people {{come down with}} the [[illness]], they often have [[long-lasting]] [[diarrhea]] and stomach pain. The [[infection]], which doctors call cyclosporiasis, is not usually dangerous. Still, some patients {{end up}} needing [[medical care]] to {{deal with}} their [[symptoms]].

verbs.wrong: To pass an illness to another person
verbs.correct: To become sick with an illness
verbs.why: A traveler might come down with a stomach bug, and a whole office might come down with the same cold. In this outbreak, people come down with cyclospora after eating produce grown with dirty water.

chunks.text: Health officials say the [[germs]] can get onto fresh food when [[irrigation]] water on farms is dirty. The CDC is {{looking into}} the outbreak, and its scientists are {{carrying out}} tests to learn more about it. Officials also [[warn of]] [[the danger of]] eating unwashed produce. They want people to be careful at home.

Cooking vegetables can {{cut down on}} the [[risk]] of getting sick too.

lines.text: [[Quick warning]] before dinner. Wash your vegetables really well.
Why, what happened?
A tiny parasite has {{broken out}} across the US. Over 1,000 people have gotten sick this year.
A parasite? [[Gross]]. Where does it come from?
Mostly fresh fruits and vegetables. Officials are still trying to {{find out}} which foods are contaminated. The problem is you can't see it, it's microscopic.
What happens if you {{come down with}} it?
Long-lasting diarrhea and stomach pain. It's usually not dangerous, but some people {{end up}} needing medical care to {{deal with}} the symptoms.
So how do we stay safe?
{{Wash off}} everything under running water. That helps {{get rid of}} many germs, though not every single one.
Not every one? [[Comforting]].
Cooking your vegetables can {{cut down on}} the risk too. And the CDC is {{looking into}} it, their scientists are {{carrying out}} tests right now.
Okay. Salad washed twice tonight.

chunks.text: A dangerous [[heat wave]] {{heated up}} much of the United States over the July 4 holiday weekend. A large [[heat dome]] [[settled]] over the country, and the [[extreme]] heat {{set in}} from the Midwest to the East Coast. Officials said about 40 million people were under a heat [[alert]] on Sunday. Weather [[forecasters]] [[warned of]] a serious danger to people's health.

chunks.text: Forecasters said the heat wave [[broke many old records]]. Temperatures {{shot up}} above 100 degrees Fahrenheit in many cities. lines.text: Remember that heat wave over the July 4 weekend? The numbers are [[unbelievable]].
I heard it was bad. How bad?
The whole country {{heated up}} at once. The extreme heat {{set in}} from the Midwest to the East Coast, and 40 million people were under a heat alert.
Forty million? [[Seriously?]]
Temperatures {{shot up}} past 100 degrees in many cities. Washington hit 103, a new record.
What about the nights? It usually gets better [[after dark]].
Not this time. The air didn't {{cool down}} overnight, so people couldn't {{cool off}} at all. It stayed near 80.
That's the dangerous part, right?
Exactly. At least 24 people died. Officials {{pointed out}} that extreme heat is one of the deadliest kinds of weather.
What did they tell people to do?
To {{carry on}} drinking water, rest indoors, and {{look out for}} older neighbors. Cities opened cooling centers to help people {{deal with}} it, and some outdoor events were {{called off}}.
Did it ever end?
[[Thankfully]], yes. The heat finally {{let up}} when cooler air arrived.

stories.headline: New cells bring back sight in mice

chunks.text: Scientists at Duke University said they had {{carried out}} an [[exciting]] experiment. A team led by Professor Sharon Gerecht {{set out}} to grow tiny blood vessels for the [[retina]] using [[stem cells]]. These special cells are very hard to make, but the scientists {{came up with}} a [[clever]] way to grow them in the lab. Their [[goal]] was to help people who are slowly [[losing their sight]].

verbs.wrong: To promise to finish something important

verbs.why: Explorers set out on long journeys, and researchers set out to answer a hard question. The Duke team set out to grow the delicate blood vessels found in the retina.

chunks.text: The researchers used stem cells that can [[turn into]] almost any cell in the body. In the lab, these cells slowly grew into the [[tissue]] that [[lines]] the blood vessels in the eye. To copy eye disease, the team put the tissue [[under stress]], and it started to {{break down}} [[in the same way]] it does in sick patients. These blood vessel tissue cells normally come only from inside the body, so growing them outside the body in the lab was a real [[breakthrough]].

verbs.wrong: To grow larger and stronger
verbs.correct: To stop working or collapse
verbs.why: Old cars break down on the highway, and a diet plan can break down after a few weeks. Under stress, the lab grown eye tissue broke down the same way it does in sick patients.

chunks.text: Next, the team tested the new cells in mice, not in people. They [[injected]] the cells into mice with weak, [[damaged]] eyes. The cells joined the tissue and {{built up}} strong, healthy blood vessels. This slowly {{brought the animals' sight back}}, and their [[vision]] got better. Mice that were treated early did not {{end up}} completely [[blind]].

verbs.wrong: To replace old cells with donor tissue
verbs.correct: To make something grow stronger
verbs.why: Regular training builds up muscle, and steady saving builds up a bank account over time. Inside the treated mice, the new cells built up strong, healthy blood vessels.

chunks.text: Professor Gerecht said the results [[point to]] a [[hopeful]] future, but she was [[careful]]. [[So far]] the [[method]] has only been tested in mice, so scientists cannot say yet that it will work in humans. They still need to work on safety before any tests in people. Doctors do not {{rule out}} problems, and they say a real [[treatment]] for [[diabetic retinopathy]], [[a leading cause]] of [[blindness]], may still be many [[years away]].

lines.text: [[Here's some good news]] from science. Researchers {{brought back}} sight in blind mice.
[[No way]]. How did they do that?
With stem cells. A team at Duke {{set out}} to grow tiny blood vessels for the eye, and they {{carried out}} the whole experiment in their lab.
I thought cells like that were impossible to grow outside the body.
Almost impossible. But the scientists {{came up with}} a clever way to do it.
And it worked?
First they copied eye disease in the lab, and the tissue began to {{break down}} just like in sick patients. Then they injected healthy new cells into mice with damaged eyes.
[[Poor mice]]. What happened?
The cells {{built up}} strong new blood vessels, and the animals' sight slowly returned. Mice treated early didn't {{end up}} blind at all.
[[That actually gives me hope]]. Could it help people one day?
Maybe, but the scientists are careful. They don't {{rule out}} problems, and a real treatment could still be [[years away]].

mainIdea.s: Italy's national rail operator plans to expand high-speed service between several major cities over the next five years. The project will cost billions of euros and create thousands of new jobs.

A Swiss start-up. They {{set up}} a test track in Switzerland last year, 48 panels right between the rails.

mainIdea.s: Rescuers pulled a security guard out of a collapsed parking lot alive after eight days. A strong concrete booth had protected him, and teams from seven countries dug for 70 hours.

lines.text: Did you hear about the man in Venezuela? The one they {{pulled out}} of a collapsed building?

stories.headline: Giraffes can do simple math

sources.title: Study finds giraffes may be capable of rudimentary math - UPI
Giraffes combine quantities similarly to addition - University of Barcelona
Giraffes combine quantities similarly to addition - Phys.org
9@9: Giraffes can do math (video, WGN Living)

chunks.text: Scientists have {{found out}} that giraffes can do simple math. [[Researchers]] at the University of Barcelona {{carried out}} a study with four giraffes at a zoo in Spain. They wanted to see [[whether]] the animals could {{work out}} which [[amount]] of food was bigger. The results [[surprised]] many people.

verbs.wrong: To share a fact with the public
verbs.correct: To learn or discover something
verbs.why: You check the mail to find out if a package arrived, and a quick search can find out a restaurant's hours. Scientists at the University of Barcelona found out that giraffes can do simple math.

verbs.wrong: To plan something in detail
verbs.correct: To do or perform a task
verbs.why: Doctors carry out tests before a surgery, and a company can carry out a survey to learn what customers want. Researchers at the University of Barcelona carried out a study with four giraffes at a zoo in Spain.

verbs.wrong: To smell the difference in food type
verbs.correct: To find the answer to something
verbs.why: You work out a fair price for a used car, and kids work out how to split candy evenly between friends. The scientists wanted to see if the giraffes could work out which pile of food was bigger.

chunks.text: In the test, the scientists {{set up}} [[clear]] [[containers]] with different numbers of carrot and vegetable pieces. Sometimes they added more pieces, and sometimes they {{took away}} a few. Each time, the giraffes had to {{pick out}} the container with more food. To get the [[reward]], the animals used their long [[tongues]] to reach it.

verbs.wrong: To hide something from view
verbs.correct: To prepare or arrange something
verbs.why: You set up chairs before a party, and a photographer might set up lights before a shoot. The scientists set up clear containers holding different numbers of carrot and vegetable pieces.

verbs.wrong: To put things in a row
verbs.correct: To remove something
verbs.why: A waiter takes away empty plates at the end of a meal, and a nurse might take away an old bandage. Sometimes the scientists added pieces of food, and sometimes they took away a few.

verbs.wrong: To point at something you want
verbs.correct: To choose one thing from several
verbs.why: You pick out a birthday card at the store, and a shopper can pick out the ripest fruit from a pile. Each time, the giraffes had to pick out the container that held more food to earn a reward.

chunks.text: When the scientists added pieces, the giraffes did [[far better]] than [[luck]] [[alone]] would explain. [[According to the study]], they chose the larger amount about 68 percent of the time. This helped the team {{rule out}} the idea that the animals were only [[guessing]]. The results [[suggest]] giraffes can {{keep track of}} small numbers and can {{tell apart}} large and small amounts of food. However, the animals could not [[solve]] harder tasks, [[such as]] [[subtraction]].

verbs.wrong: To show that an idea is only partly true
verbs.correct: To decide that something is not possible
verbs.why: A mechanic can rule out a battery problem after a quick test, and a doctor might rule out a serious illness with one scan. The strong results helped the team rule out the idea that the giraffes were only guessing.

verbs.wrong: To multiply two numbers together quickly
verbs.correct: To follow the number or progress of something
verbs.why: You keep track of your spending in a small notebook, and a coach keeps track of the score during a close game. The results suggest giraffes can keep track of small numbers of carrots and vegetables too.

verbs.wrong: To choose the thing that you like best
verbs.correct: To see the difference between things
verbs.why: Twins can be hard to tell apart at first glance, and a new driver might struggle to tell apart the brake and the gas pedal. The study suggests giraffes can tell apart large and small amounts of food.

chunks.text: [[For a long time]], people thought that only humans and a few [[clever]] animals, such as [[primates]] and crows, had [[a sense of]] numbers. This new study adds to [[a growing list]] of animals that can count [[in some way]]. The researchers now want to {{carry on}} their work with other zoo animals. They hope it will help us {{figure out}} more about how animal minds work.

verbs.correct: To continue doing something
verbs.why: A band can carry on playing even after the lights dim, and a runner might carry on despite heavy rain. The researchers now want to carry on their work by testing other zoo animals too.

mainIdea.s: Four giraffes usually chose the container with more food, so it seems they can tell small numbers apart. They could not do harder math, such as subtraction.
mainIdea.why: They picked the larger amount about 68 percent of the time, which is better than guessing. But the study says they could not solve harder tasks such as subtraction.

mainIdea.s: Zoos in Spain have started giving giraffes puzzle feeders to keep their minds busy. Keepers say the animals now eat more slowly and seem much calmer.

lines.text: Okay, [[weird question]]. Do you think a giraffe can count?
...What?
I just read about it. Scientists in Barcelona {{found out}} giraffes can do simple math. They {{carried out}} a whole study at a zoo.
[[Come on]]. How do you even test a giraffe?
They {{set up}} containers with carrot pieces, and the giraffes had to {{pick out}} the one with more food. They got it right 68 percent of the time.
Maybe they [[just got lucky]].
[[That's what I said]]! But the numbers were too good, so the scientists {{ruled out}} guessing. They think giraffes can {{keep track of}} small amounts.
Huh. So [[what's next]], giraffes doing my taxes?
They failed at subtraction, so no. But the team wants to {{carry on}} with other animals and {{figure out}} how their minds work.
[[Honestly]]? Smarter than some people I know.
